instruction: List only the regular files in this directory, skipping subdirectories.
context: Zsh glob qualifiers: a parenthesised suffix filters matches by attribute. The dot qualifier keeps only regular files, so directories, symlinks, and sockets are excluded before ls ever sees them. Bash has no equivalent and needs find.

instruction: List only the directories here, one per line.
context: Zsh glob qualifiers: the slash qualifier keeps only directories. -d stops ls from descending into each one and -1 forces single-column output.

instruction: Show the single most recently modified file in this directory.
context: Zsh glob qualifiers: om sorts matches by modification time, newest first, and [1] takes the first element of that sorted list. Capital Om reverses to oldest first. This replaces the fragile ls -t | head -1 pipeline.

instruction: Show the three oldest files in this directory.
context: Zsh glob qualifiers: capital Om sorts by modification time oldest first, and [1,3] slices the first three matches. The subscript range is inclusive on both ends and is applied after sorting.

instruction: List files in this directory that are larger than ten megabytes.
context: Zsh glob qualifiers: L filters on file length, the unit letter m means megabytes, and + means strictly greater than. Lk is kilobytes and Lg is gigabytes; a bare L counts bytes.

instruction: Delete every zero-byte file in the current directory.
context: Zsh glob qualifiers: L0 matches a length of exactly zero bytes and the dot restricts to regular files, so an empty directory is not caught. The bare -- protects against filenames that begin with a dash.

instruction: List files modified within the last hour.
context: Zsh glob qualifiers: m filters on modification time, h selects hours as the unit, and a minus means less than that many units ago. mh+24 would instead mean older than a day.

instruction: Count the lines in every Python file anywhere below the current directory.
context: Zsh: ** matches across directory levels, so **/*.py finds Python files at any depth including the current one. The dot qualifier drops anything that is not a regular file, which prevents a directory named like a source file from breaking the command.

instruction: Find every executable regular file below the scripts directory.
context: Zsh glob qualifiers: x tests the execute permission for the owner and the dot restricts to regular files, so directories, which are always traversable, do not match.

instruction: Remove any .tmp files here without erroring when there are none.
context: Zsh glob qualifiers: N enables nullglob for this pattern alone, so a pattern matching nothing expands to zero words instead of raising 'no matches found'. This is the per-pattern alternative to setopt nullglob.

instruction: List everything in this directory including hidden dotfiles.
context: Zsh glob qualifiers: D makes the pattern match names beginning with a dot, which globs normally skip. It applies only to this pattern, unlike setopt globdots which changes every glob in the shell.

instruction: Find files in /etc owned by root.
context: Zsh glob qualifiers: u selects by owner and takes a numeric uid or a name in delimiters, so u0 is root. The parallel g qualifier filters by group.

instruction: Find symbolic links in this tree whose target no longer exists.
context: Zsh glob qualifiers: @ matches symbolic links and the leading minus makes the qualifiers that follow test the link target rather than the link. Combined, -@ identifies links that still resolve to a link, and dangling links are what remain when the target check fails.

instruction: List every Markdown file here except the README.
context: Zsh extended globbing: the tilde operator subtracts a pattern from the matches on its left. This requires setopt extended_glob, which oh-my-zsh and most frameworks enable by default.

instruction: Find readme files regardless of their capitalization.
context: Zsh extended globbing: (#i) is a globbing flag that makes the rest of the pattern case-insensitive. Flags are positional and apply from where they appear onward. Requires setopt extended_glob.

instruction: List all the C and header files in this directory.
context: Zsh: parentheses with a pipe express alternation inside a glob, matching either extension. Unlike brace expansion this only produces names that actually exist, so it never yields a nonexistent path.

instruction: Turn on Zsh's extended globbing features for this session.
context: Zsh: extended_glob enables the ~, ^, and (#...) pattern operators. Option names are case-insensitive and ignore underscores, so extendedglob and EXTENDED_GLOB are the same option. unsetopt reverses it.

instruction: Stop Zsh from erroring when a glob matches nothing.
context: Zsh: by default an unmatched glob is a fatal error, unlike Bash which passes the pattern through literally. null_glob makes it expand to nothing instead; the per-pattern form is the (N) qualifier.

instruction: Capture command output into an array with one element per line.
context: Zsh parameter expansion flags: (f) splits the value on newlines into separate words. The command substitution is quoted so it is not word-split on spaces first, which is what preserves entries containing spaces. print -l prints one word per line.

instruction: Split the PATH variable on colons and print each entry on its own line.
context: Zsh parameter expansion flags: (s.X.) splits the value on the string X, where the delimiter characters around it can be any unused pair. This is the general form of the newline-splitting (f) flag.

instruction: Join the elements of the path array into one comma-separated string.
context: Zsh parameter expansion flags: (j:X:) joins an array's elements with the separator X, the inverse of (s:X:). print -r disables escape interpretation so backslashes in the values survive.

instruction: Print the entries of PATH with duplicates removed, preserving order.
context: Zsh parameter expansion flags: (u) removes duplicate elements while keeping the first occurrence's position, unlike sort -u which reorders. The path array is Zsh's tied array view of the PATH string.

instruction: Print a variable's value converted to upper case.
context: Zsh parameter expansion flags: (U) upcases and (L) downcases the expansion. (C) capitalizes each word. These avoid a round trip through tr for simple case changes.

instruction: Print just the filename portion of a path held in a variable.
context: Zsh history modifiers: :t is the tail, equivalent to basename, and :h is the head, equivalent to dirname. They operate on the string without spawning a process.

instruction: Strip the extension from a filename stored in a variable.
context: Zsh history modifiers: :r removes the extension leaving the root, and :e yields the extension alone. They chain, so ${file:t:r} gives the basename without its suffix.

instruction: Expand a relative path variable to a full absolute path.
context: Zsh history modifiers: :A resolves the path to an absolute form and resolves symbolic links, similar to realpath. :a makes it absolute without resolving links.

instruction: Print a configuration value, falling back to a default when it is unset or empty.
context: Parameter expansion: :- substitutes the default when the variable is unset or empty, while a bare - substitutes only when it is unset. Neither form assigns; use := to also store the default.

instruction: Fail loudly in a script when a required environment variable is missing.
context: Parameter expansion: :? writes the given message to stderr and aborts the shell when the variable is unset or empty. This is the terse way to assert required configuration at the top of a script.

instruction: Print the PATH entries that are not inside /usr.
context: Zsh parameter expansion: :# removes array elements matching the pattern, and :| subtracts another array's elements. Applied to a scalar it removes the value entirely when it matches.

instruction: Print how many entries are in the PATH.
context: Zsh: ${#array} is the element count, whereas ${#scalar} is the character length. Zsh arrays are one-indexed by default, unlike Bash's zero-indexed arrays, which is a frequent porting bug.

instruction: Print the first three entries of the PATH array.
context: Zsh: array subscripts start at 1 and a comma-separated pair is an inclusive range, so [1,3] is the first three elements. Negative indices count from the end, so [-1] is the last.

instruction: Print a variable with shell quoting applied so it can be safely re-evaluated.
context: Zsh parameter expansion flags: (q) adds the quoting needed for the value to survive another round of shell parsing, and (qq) and (qqq) select specific quote styles. This is the safe way to build a command string.

instruction: Rename every .txt file in this directory to .md using pattern capture.
context: Zsh: zmv is an autoloaded function that renames using glob patterns, where parenthesised groups become $1, $2, and so on in the replacement. Both arguments must be quoted so zmv sees the patterns rather than their expansion. Load it with autoload -Uz zmv.

instruction: Preview a bulk rename before actually moving anything.
context: Zsh: zmv -n is a dry run that prints each intended rename without performing it. -i prompts per file and -f forces overwriting. Running -n first is the standard guard against a bad capture group.

instruction: Lowercase the extension of every JPG file anywhere in the tree.
context: Zsh: (**/) captures the directory prefix at any depth, including the empty case, so the rename stays within each file's own directory. Each parenthesised group takes the next positional variable.

instruction: Load the zmv function so it is available in this shell.
context: Zsh: autoload marks a function to be loaded from fpath on first use. -U suppresses alias expansion inside the function and -z forces Zsh-style parsing; the -Uz pair is the standard idiom for shipped functions.

instruction: Emit the matching filenames NUL-separated so they can be piped safely.
context: Zsh: print -N separates output words with NUL bytes instead of newlines, which pairs with xargs -0. -r disables escape processing and the (.N) qualifiers keep regular files while tolerating no matches.

instruction: Declare an integer variable in a Zsh script.
context: Zsh: typeset -i declares an integer, so arithmetic assignments are evaluated automatically. -a declares an array, -A an associative array, and -r makes the variable read-only.

instruction: Create an associative array mapping environment names to hostnames.
context: Zsh: typeset -A declares an associative array, and the initializer alternates keys and values as a flat list rather than using Bash's [key]=value syntax. Read a value with $hosts[staging].

instruction: Find out whether ls is an alias, a function, or a real binary.
context: Zsh: whence -v describes how a name would be resolved, and -a shows every match rather than only the first. This is the Zsh-native form of type -a and is more informative than which, which only reports paths.

instruction: Show the last twenty commands from shell history with their numbers.
context: Zsh: fc -l lists history entries, and a negative number selects that many of the most recent. fc -e opens an entry in the editor for correction, which is what the built-in history editing relies on.

instruction: Show the five largest files anywhere below this directory.
context: Zsh glob qualifiers: OL sorts by length descending, oL sorts ascending, and the [1,5] subscript takes the top five after sorting. The dot keeps directories out of the ranking.

instruction: Audit this tree for files that are writable by anyone.
context: Zsh glob qualifiers: capital W matches world-writable files, while lowercase w tests writability by the current user. R, W, and X test the other-permission bits, which is exactly what a permissions audit needs.

instruction: Show the most recently modified file in the Downloads folder on macOS.
context: Zsh glob qualifiers work identically on macOS because they are a shell feature, not a coreutils one. Since Catalina, Zsh is the default login shell on macOS, so om[1] needs no extra setup.

instruction: List only regular files in the current directory on macOS.
context: Zsh: the dot glob qualifier is provided by the shell, so it behaves the same on macOS as on Linux even though ls itself is the BSD implementation with different flags.

instruction: Count how many Python files exist anywhere below this directory.
context: Zsh: the glob expands to one word per match and print -l puts each on its own line for wc to count. The (N) qualifier yields zero words instead of a fatal 'no matches found' when the tree has no Python files.

instruction: Make a pipeline in a script fail when any stage fails, not just the last one.
context: Zsh: pipe_fail makes a pipeline's exit status the rightmost non-zero one, so a failing producer is not masked by a succeeding consumer. err_exit aborts on any uncaught failure, matching Bash's set -e.
